I am a researcher working at the intersection of machine learning and natural language processing. My work focuses on building systems that can understand and generate human language with greater robustness and fairness.

I received my Ph.D. in Computer Science from Example University, where I was advised by Dr. Ada Lovelace. Before that, I completed my M.S. in Computational Linguistics and my B.S. in Mathematics.

My research has been published at venues including ACL, EMNLP, NeurIPS, and ICML. I have also served as a reviewer for these conferences and as an area chair for ACL 2024.

I am always interested in collaborations. If you are working on something related, feel free to reach out.

## Natural Language Understanding

My primary research line investigates how neural networks represent and process semantic meaning. I am particularly interested in compositional generalization — the ability of models to systematically combine known concepts in novel ways. This includes work on semantic parsing, logical inference, and structured prediction tasks where models must reason over explicit representations.

## Robustness and Fairness

A second focus of my research is on making NLP systems more robust and fair. I study how models behave under distribution shift, adversarial perturbations, and demographic variation. The goal is to develop evaluation protocols and training methods that yield systems which perform reliably across diverse populations and use cases.

## Efficient Learning

I also work on methods for learning with limited supervision, including few-shot learning, active learning, and self-supervised pretraining. I am interested in understanding what makes pretraining effective and how we can design better learning objectives that reduce the need for large labeled datasets.

Efficient Few-Shot Learning for Structured Prediction
Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
Juan María Herrera-López, Bob Chen, Sarah Lee
We propose a meta-learning approach for few-shot structured prediction that achieves strong results with minimal labeled data. Our method combines prototypical networks with structured output spaces.

Evaluating Robustness Under Distribution Shift in Question Answering
Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)

We present a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the robustness of question answering systems under natural distribution shifts. Our analysis reveals that current state-of-the-art models degrade significantly when tested on out-of-domain data.

Some thoughts on why models struggle with systematic compositionality.

After working on compositional generalization for several years, I keep coming back to the same question: why do neural networks fail at systematic compositionality when humans do it effortlessly?

The standard explanation is that training data lacks the right diversity. But I think the issue runs deeper. Current architectures may lack the inductive biases necessary for compositional reasoning.
